attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Correctly links the incentives sentence to the preceding near-term moratorium sentence and keeps the list of groups. The parenthetical hedges whether the economics will pay off, not the causal claim, so the claim stays firm.

contract.note: The plain reading (financial incentives materially blocked a broad pause) is the ordinary one. It is fair to require decision-linked evidence rather than proof that incentives merely exist.

evidence.note: a16z's self-statement (Dec 2023) of donation intent against restrictive candidates. It shows an influence channel but does not link that channel to any moratorium decision.

UK PM speech (Oct 2023), a government primary statement labelled as a disclosure. It gives pro-innovation and uncertainty reasons for restraint, an alternative explanation, but does not settle causation.

reviews.rationale: Neither item connects financial incentives to an actual moratorium decision. e1 shows investor political intent. e2 offers alternative stated reasons. Neither confirms nor rules out the asserted causal role, so the packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: "Obviously never going to" is a firm, unhedged forecast. The normalisation keeps the near-term scope.

contract.note: Marcus gave no endpoint for "near-term", and the contract declines to invent one. Scoring therefore turns on the horizon reading. The asymmetry (an early moratorium could contradict the forecast, but nothing can support it) follows from the missing deadline.

evidence.note: FLI (an advocacy group, Mar 2024) reports targeted firms had not paused. This is consistent with the forecast for the first months, but it is not exhaustive and supplies no endpoint.
CRS (Jun 2025): no broad US federal AI prohibitions had been enacted. This covers one jurisdiction only.
Seoul commitments (May 2024) are risk-contingent and voluntary, not a broad development moratorium. Labelled as a company disclosure although it is a government publication.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no stated deadline. No qualifying broad moratorium appears in the packet, so the early-contradiction rule is not met. Without a source-grounded endpoint the forecast cannot be scored as supported, so it remains unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. e2 relies on Hawley's question, not Marcus's testimony.

semantics.note: Captures both parts: a vast worldwide increase in AI-policy attention, and partial credit to the letter.

contract.note: Treating "some credit" as a modest contribution and "vastly more" as a substantial, broad increase is an ordinary and fair reading.

evidence.note: First-ever UN Security Council AI debate (Jul 2023). It indicates new international attention within the period but is not a matched before/after measure and is not tied to the letter.
Senate hearing (May 2023): a senator raised the letter and asked witnesses about it. This shows the letter entered policy deliberation, a modest contribution.
AI Index data on policy activity rising before 2023. No matched March–September comparison.

reviews.rationale: e2 supports the letter getting some credit. The "vastly more, throughout the world" increase rests on a single UN debate, with no comparable before/after measure, which the contract requires. The increase is suggestive but not established, and nothing contradicts it, so the claim is unresolved overall.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The normalisation omits "remain unreliable" explicitly, but that is implied by the hallucination and reasoning parts. It is a faithful present-state observation.

contract.note: The plain reading (unchecked outputs are not dependable; not every answer is wrong) is ordinary. Taking the reporting window from the post's six-month title is reasonable.

evidence.note: FActScore (May 2023): ChatGPT factual precision of about 58% on biographies. Substantial unsupported content within the window.
Valmeekam et al. (May 2023): GPT-4 at about 34% on Blocksworld planning. Substantial reasoning failures, though improved over older models and helped by external verifiers.

reviews.rationale: Within the window, independent evaluations document both unsupported factual output (e1) and substantial reasoning failures (e2) in leading LLMs, which meets the support condition. The gains from external tools noted in e2 limit the claim's scope but do not contradict it.
